title: Flock Safety’s Feature Updates Cannot Make Automated License Plate Readers Safe
summary: EFF criticizes Flock Safety's response to recent controversies—including a Texas sheriff's use of its ALPR network to track an abortion seeker and informal data sharing with ICE—arguing that promised feature updates and reliance on local agency policies cannot mitigate the harms of its nationwide surveillance network. The article urges communities to follow cities like Austin, Denver, and San Diego in pushing back against Flock deployments.

key_quotes.quote: a sheriff's office in Texas searched data from more than 83,000 automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras to track down a woman suspected of self-managing an abortion.

more than 4,000 nation and statewide lookups by local and state police done either at the behest of the federal government or as an 'informal' favor to federal law enforcement, or with a potential immigration focus.
Flock operates as a single point of failure that can compromise—and has compromised—the privacy of millions of Americans simultaneously.
the only feature update we can truly rely on to protect people's rights and safety is no network at all.

title: Washington Court Rules That Data Captured on Flock Safety Cameras Are Public Records
summary: A Skagit County (WA) Superior Court ruled that ALPR images captured by Flock Safety cameras for the cities of Stanwood and Sedro-Woolley are public records under Washington's Public Records Act, rejecting the cities' arguments that data stored on Flock's servers wasn't a public record until accessed. Despite the ruling, requester Jose Rodriguez won't receive the footage because the cities allowed it to auto-delete during litigation. EFF situates the ruling amid broader scrutiny of Flock, including ICE/CBP data sharing and the El Cajon AG lawsuit.

key_quotes.quote: The Flock images generated by the Flock cameras...are public records
data generated by Flock [automated license plate reader cameras (ALPRs)] and stored in the Flock cloud system are not public records unless and until a public agency extracts and downloads that data.
The cities both allowed the records to be automatically deleted after I submitted my records requests and while they decided to have their legal council review my request.

title: EFF's Investigations Expose Flock Safety's Surveillance Abuses: 2025 in Review
summary: EFF's year-in-review summarizes its 2025 investigations into Flock Safety's nationwide ALPR network, documenting agency searches tied to protests, racially biased searches targeting Romani people, and Texas deputies querying Flock data in an abortion-related investigation. The piece highlights resulting congressional and state investigations, an Illinois audit, an ACLU/EFF lawsuit against San Jose PD, municipal cancellations of Flock contracts, and concerns about Flock's expansion into audio 'distress' detection.

key_quotes.quote: more than 80 law enforcement agencies used language perpetuating harmful stereotypes against Romani people when searching the nationwide Flock Safety ALPR network
A Johnson County official ran two searches with the note "had an abortion, search for female." The second search probed 6,809 networks, accessing 83,345 cameras across nearly the entire country.
SJPD and other California law enforcement agencies searched San Jose's database 3,965,519 times
Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias launched an audit after EFF research showed Flock allowed U.S. Customs and Border Protection to access Illinois data in violation of state privacy laws.

title: Oakland’s License Plate Camera Contract Is Back Up for a Vote. Critics Are Crying Foul | KQED
summary: Oakland's City Council is set to vote on a two-year, $2.25 million contract extension with Flock Safety after the Rules Committee revived the proposal following its failure in the Public Safety Committee. Critics, including Councilmember Carroll Fife, the ACLU, and the Privacy Advisory Commission, oppose the deal citing Flock's data-sharing with federal agencies including ICE, which violates state law and Oakland's sanctuary city policy.

key_quotes.quote: I'm deeply concerned that this process feels like it lacks transparency and democracy

more than 4,000 Oakland residents have urged the council to vote no on Flock expansion, and more than 40 organizations, including the ACLU of Northern California and multiple local unions, submitted a joint letter

State law prohibits local law enforcement from sharing automated license plate data with out-of-state and federal agencies, and Oakland's sanctuary city policy bars police and city officials from aiding in immigration enforcement.
In November, the nonprofit Secure Justice and its leader, Brian Hofer, sued Oakland over the reports of data sharing.
this vendor has shown time and time again that they will just thwart the rule of law in cities and states all over the nation

title: Santa Cruz the First in California to Terminate Its Contract With Flock Safety | KQED
summary: The Santa Cruz City Council voted 6-1 to terminate its contract with Flock Safety, becoming the first California city to do so, citing reports that out-of-state agencies accessed its ALPR data on behalf of federal immigration enforcement in apparent violation of California's SB 34. Advocates documented roughly 4,000 such queries between June and October 2025; Flock said sharing settings can be customized by any city.

key_quotes.quote: For us, the threat to our civil liberties was greater than any benefit we could get from the flawed product
California for 10 years has prohibited the sharing of license plate data out of state. Ten years!

between June and October 2025, state agencies accessed Santa Cruz camera data roughly 4,000 times on behalf of federal law enforcement, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, in violation of California's SB 34
the typical standard Flock contract, which the agencies in Santa Cruz County all signed, enables nationwide sharing, and nationwide sharing was going on the entire time
Santa Cruz joins nearly two dozen jurisdictions in 2025 that canceled or rejected Flock contracts by exercising procurement power

title: San José Is the Latest Bay Area City to Restrict Flock License Plate Cameras | KQED
summary: The San José City Council unanimously voted to tighten restrictions on its 474-camera Flock Safety ALPR network, reducing data retention from one year to 30 days, banning camera placement near reproductive health facilities, places of worship, gender-affirming care facilities and consulates, prohibiting facial recognition integration, and directing the city manager to explore alternative vendors. Advocates including SIREN and CAIR, who have sued the city, said the changes don't go far enough and want San José to terminate its Flock contract entirely, as Santa Cruz and Mountain View have done.

key_quotes.quote: I have never seen a technology advance so impactful to our ability to keep the community safe as I have with these license plate reader cameras

The city's changes reduce the default data retention period from one year to 30 days, prohibit placing cameras near reproductive health care facilities and places of worship, and add new documentation and authentication requirements for agencies requesting access to the data.
We must refuse to give this authoritarian federal government any AI mass surveillance weapon that will and has already been used to hunt our neighbors
My concern is not with ALPR technology itself; my concern is with Flock Safety as a vendor

title: City Learns Flock Accessed Cameras in Children's Gymnastics Room as a Sales Pitch Demo, Renews Contract Anyway
summary: Dunwoody, Georgia residents discovered via public-records requests that Flock Safety employees accessed local cameras—including those in a children's gymnastics room, pool, and Jewish community center—as part of sales demos to other police departments. Flock confirmed the access occurred under a 'demo partner program' but disputed characterizations that employees were spying, and said it will now restrict demos to more public locations. The city renewed its Flock contract despite the controversy.

key_quotes.quote: sales employees at Flock have been accessing sensitive cameras in the town to demonstrate the company's surveillance technology to police departments around the country
The cities involved in this program have authorized select Flock employees to demonstrate new products and features as we develop them in partnership with the city.
We have therefore determined that employees will be trained to only conduct demos in more public locations, like retail parking lots

title: Flock Removes States From National Lookup Tool After ICE and Abortion Searches Revealed
summary: Flock has disabled national lookup access to its ALPR cameras in California, Illinois, and Virginia following 404 Media reporting that out-of-state agencies were searching cameras on behalf of ICE and for an abortion-related investigation, and after new Virginia legislation. The Illinois Secretary of State is investigating potential violations of state sharing laws.

key_quotes.quote: Flock, the automatic license plate reader (ALPR) company with a presence in thousands of communities across the U.S., has stopped agencies across the country from searching cameras inside Illinois, California, and Virginia
This practice violates multiple state laws which bar the sharing of ALPR data out of state or it being accessed for immigration or healthcare purposes.
The Illinois Secretary of State is investigating whether Illinois police departments broke the law by sharing data with outside agencies for immigration or abortion related reasons.

title: San Diegans Push Back on Flock ALPR Surveillance
summary: EFF reports on the TRUST Coalition's campaign urging San Diego's city council to end its Flock Safety ALPR contract ahead of the program's first annual review. The piece highlights alleged sharing of ALPR data with federal agencies including HSI and CBP, deployments at Comic-Con and Pride without required council approval, the Privacy Board's recommendation to reject the Surveillance Use Policy, and the program's $3.5M annual cost.

key_quotes.quote: San Diego Police have reportedly disclosed license plate data to federal agencies— including Homeland Security Investigations and Customs and Border Patrol.

despite a local ordinance requiring city council approval before deployment of surveillance technology, San Diego police have reportedly deployed ALPRs and smart streetlights at Comic-Con and Pride without the required approval
The San Diego Privacy Board recently recommended the city reject the Surveillance Use Policy for this technology.
ALPRs like Flock’s don’t prevent crime—they just vacuum up data on everyone who drives past.

title: Victory! Austin Organizers Cancel City's Flock ALPR Contract
summary: EFF celebrates Austin organizers' successful effort to block renewal of the city's Flock Safety ALPR contract, ending Austin police use of the network at month's end. A pre-vote audit found over 20% of ALPR searches lacked proper documentation and that contract terms permitted retention and sharing beyond council limits. Austin still uses ALPRs via an Axon contract.

key_quotes.quote: an audit of the Austin Police Department program also revealed that over 20% of ALPR database searches lacked proper documentation or justification, in violation of department policy
The audit also revealed contract language allowed for data retention beyond council-mandated limits on retention and potential sharing with outside agencies.
While the Flock contract has been discontinued, Austin still makes use of ALPRs via its contract with Axon

title: EFFecting Change: Get the Flock Out of Our City

agency_candidates.display_name: North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation (NCSBI)

summary: EFF announces a February 19, 2026 livestream event discussing growing resistance to Flock Safety's ALPR contracts across U.S. cities, featuring speakers from EFF, Fight for the Future, and Rural Privacy Coalition. The post argues Flock cameras enable surveillance of abortion seekers, protesters, and marginalized communities, and highlights jurisdictions rejecting Flock deployments.

key_quotes.quote: Flock contracts have quietly spread to cities across the country. But Flock ALPR (Automated License Plate Readers) erode civil liberties from the moment they're installed.
From Austin to Cambridge to small towns across Texas, jurisdictions are rejecting Flock contracts altogether, proving that surveillance isn't inevitable—it's a choice.

title: As California Cities Grow Wary of Flock Safety Cameras, Mountain View Shuts Its Off | KQED
summary: Mountain View Police Department turned off its Flock Safety ALPR cameras after an audit revealed federal agencies accessed its data via a national lookup feature in 2024 and 29 of 30 cameras were accessed by unapproved California agencies, violating a 2015 state law. The decision follows similar terminations by Santa Cruz, Los Altos Hills and over two dozen other US municipalities amid concerns about ICE access to Flock data, while the city council will decide the program's future at a month-end meeting.

key_quotes.quote: Community trust is more important than any individual tool. I share your anger and frustration regarding how Flock Safety's system enabled out-of-state agencies to search our license plate data, and I am sorry that such searches occurred.

The department said the feature was "enabled without MVPD's permission or knowledge." It also said that 29 of its 30 cameras were accessed by other California law enforcement agencies that had not been approved to do so.
What did Flock do? Did Flock force a code change on you and lie to you about it? Statistically, it's most likely to be the Mountain View Police Department that turned those things on.
In California, a 2015 state law prohibits state and local law enforcement agencies from sharing license plate reader data with out-of-state or federal agencies.
